newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey says pulled most troops out of north Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says pulled most troops out of north Iraq.

text.p: Turkey said on Thursday it had withdrawn most of its forces from northern Iraq after a six-week campaign against Kurdish rebels that angered the Arab world.
"We have pulled back into Turkey, leaving a small amount behind," army spokesman Colonel Suleyman Canpolat told reporters in the Turkish city of Diyarbakir.
Turkey sent some 10,000 troops into northern Iraq on May 14 against Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels who use bases in the mountains there to strike into Turkey.
"We have left soldiers behind to help in the delivery and direction of air and artillery fire. We have some units on the other side of the border," he said.
Canpolat said troops had killed 3,009 guerrillas for the loss of 113 soldiers in the fighting although Western diplomats say the rebel death toll is exaggerated.
He said 49 members of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) allied to Turkey had also died. A KDP statement last week said they had lost 29 men in the fighting.
Sources close PKK put rebel losses at around 150 and say they have killed nearly 1,000 KDP and Turkish security force members.
Turkish military officials say two of its helicopters have been shot down by the PKK with Russian-made SA-7 missiles. Eleven soldiers were killed in the second helicopter attack on June 4.
"The news of the withdrawal is nothing new, it started the day after they lost the last helicopter," a spokesman for the pro-PKK Med TV said.
A Turkish military official said the guerrillas had received training in the use of the SA-7 from Turkey's traditional rival, Greece.

"With the help of a senior officer in the Greek intelligence service, a group of seven PKK members received two weeks' training on the Adriatic coast. This training was on the latest model of the SA-7," Colonel Oguz Kalelioglu said.
He said a Greek officer had been killed during the operation in the White Mountains in the far north of Iraq but gave no more details.
The entire campaign has been carried out under a strict news blackout, with correspondents barred from the region and communications blocked, making independent confirmation of events impossible.
The Arab League and some of Ankara's Western allies have condemned Turkey for its foray into the region.
Northern Iraq has been under Iraqi Kurdish control since after the end of the 1991 Gulf War but Turkey says a power vacuum there has allowed the PKK to flourish.
A Western air force shields Iraq's Kurds from any attack by Baghdad.
More than 24,000 people have died since 1984 in conflict between the army and the PKK, fighting for Kurdish self-rule in southeast Turkey.
